Sandpapergate revisited CA to set up independent committee to re-hear ball tampering testimonies
 by Cricbuzz Staff •     Share Tweet Varying recollections of the Sandpapergate have been followed by Cricket Australia setting up an independent committee © Getty Varying recollections of the Sandpapergate have been followed by Cricket Australia setting up an independent committee © Getty Cricket Australia has announced it will set up an independent committee to re-hear testimonies from players and support staff who were part of Australia’s squad during the 2018 tour of South Africa, which it hopes will serve as a ‘circuit-breaker’ to the ball-tampering saga.
 The publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr , has reopened the scars of the incident with Khawaja claiming that everyone in the team knew of the use of sandpaper. However, in the immediate aftermath of the Cape Town Test of 2018, Cricket Australia handed bans to only three players - Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft - for the incident and moved on.
 Since Khawaja’s recent revelations, while Mitchell Marsh maintained his silence, Warner and Chadd Sayers have sided with Khawaja’s version of events. Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins, meanwhile, have held their stance that the bowlers were not aware of the use of sandpaper on the ball.
 Warner has stated that the investigation of the incident by Cricket Australia was ‘shoddy’. "As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said in an Instagram post. “If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?
 “It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover-up."
 On Wednesday, CA’s chairperson David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg stated that an independent forum would be opened for players and staff who toured South Africa in 2018 to give their version of events in a ‘confidential environment’. In saying so, Greenberg insisted CA won’t be "re-prosecuting" the initial investigation of ball-tampering and no new sanctions would be handed down.
 While he stated whatever is revealed in the forum would remain confidential, it would be up to the Cricket Australia Board what information is made public. The entire exercise is expected to take about a month.
 “Over the past week we have heard several different and conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018. This has been an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and all those involved," Greenberg said. "What happened then and continues to play out now has a lot to do with the culture that existed at that time. A culture that CA played a part in creating. The recognition of that came through the commissioning of the Ethics Centre report and subsequent adoption of 36 of the 42 recommendations.
 "We are proud of the culture that the team has built over the past eight years and our players and our leaders and our coaches deserve enormous credit for that. But we recognise the pain and hurt that events surrounding Sandpapergate have caused. Let’s be honest - the game is hurting at the moment. It is not good for anyone. We need to find a path through and we need to heal.
 "As part of this process - and so that all parties who wish to - can tell their version of events we will set up an independent forum. This is a chance to give everyone a voice in an independent, safe and private setting. This is not a re-investigation, it is not designed to reprosecute or sanction. No one is compelled to participate – it is entirely up to them individually.
 "It is important to remember we are talking about events that took place more than eight years ago. We hope everyone will respect this process and the players will be given the space they need to perform at their best during an important period for the game.”
 Boon believes not reopening an investigation would allow everyone to be heard, and create a safe space for everyone to speak in a constructive and a mutually respectful manner.
 “After careful consideration, the CA Board has decided to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and perspectives,” Boon said. “We believe this is in the best interests of the game. For almost a decade, the fallout from those events has remained part of the conversation around Australian cricket. It has been a difficult chapter for many people and, increasingly, the ongoing debate has become a distraction from the game. We believe it is time for a circuit breaker.
 “This forum is not about relitigating the past. It is about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful environment, and for our sport to listen. Australian cricket is at its strongest when it is united. We owe it to everyone who loves the game to make every reasonable effort to move forward together, with understanding, respect and perspective.
 “As a former player, I know that one of the most important things cricket gives us is the relationships we build and the mateship that endures long after playing careers end. My hope is that this process can help strengthen those connections and allow us to focus on what lies ahead.
 “I would encourage everyone to allow the process to unfold respectfully and privately. We have an exciting summer of cricket ahead, and our collective focus should be on ensuring the game continues to thrive.”
